meaning: Things reach a certain (often serious) stage, and only then does someone finally act or does something change.
connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + に及んで (also に及んでも, に及び)

senses.label: Only when it came to …
senses.meaning: Things reach an extreme point before anyone finally acts. It carries criticism: “too late” or “should have happened sooner.” Written style, common in news and commentary.
senses.connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + に及んで (often with 「ようやく」, 「やっと」, 「初めて」)
examples: Only after people died did the government finally take action.
Only when things had come to this did the president finally admit responsibility.

senses.label: At this late stage
senses.meaning: The set phrase 「この期に及んで」: “even at this point, you still …?” It sounds reproachful and irritated.
senses.connection: この期（ご）に及んで（も）+ まだ〜 / 〜するのか
examples: Are you still going to make excuses at this stage?
Even now, he won't try to apologize.

senses.label: Extend to / reach
senses.meaning: 「〜に及ぶ／に及んだ」 means time, scope, or amount reaches a certain level, often “as much as.” This is the base use behind the pattern.
senses.connection: Noun (time, amount, scope) + に及ぶ / に及んだ / に及び
examples: The meeting went on until late at night.
The damage extends across the whole prefecture, and recovery is expected to take time.

notes: 「〜に及んで」 (only when it got to …) and 「〜には及ばない」 (there is no need to … / cannot match …) differ by a single 「は」 but mean completely different things: 「警察が来るに及んで」 is “only when the police arrived,” while 「来るには及ばない」 is “you need not come.”
The main clause reports an action that came too late, with an implied “it should have happened sooner.” You cannot use it for your own planned actions: ✕「卒業に及んで、海外旅行に行くつもりだ」 → ○「卒業を機に、海外旅行に行くつもりだ」.
「この期に及んで」 is a strong reproach. Saying 「この期に及んでまだ…」 to a superior or client amounts to scolding them to their face and is very rude; use it only with equals, juniors, or when talking to yourself.
「この期」 is read 「ご」, not 「き」: ✕「このきにおよんで」 → ○「このごにおよんで」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report criticizes the government for acting slowly.
daily.example: Only after the damage spread did the investigation finally begin.

daily.title: During an argument
daily.description: The other person is still making excuses at the very end.
daily.example: Are you still lying, even now?

work.title: Incident report
work.description: Explaining how a situation developed in a report.
work.example: Management only moved once the problem reached our customers.

work.title: Meeting minutes
work.description: Recording how long a meeting lasted.
work.example: The discussion lasted as long as three hours.

etymology: The te-form of the verb 「及ぶ」 (to reach, to extend to). The kanji 「及」 originally meant “to catch up with, to arrive at,” which led to the sense “a situation reaches a certain point.”

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both say that a situation has reached a certain stage, and 「〜に至って（ようやく）」 and 「〜に及んで（ようやく）」 are often interchangeable. 「に至る」 focuses more on the result of arriving at an endpoint and sounds more literary; 「に及ぶ」 also keeps the sense of time or range extending to something (「会議は深夜に及んだ」).

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built on the verb 「及ぶ」. 「〜には及ばない」 is the negative form, meaning “there is no need to …” (「ご心配には及びません」) or “cannot match …”; 「〜に及んで」 means “only when it got to ….” The two meanings are completely different, which makes them very easy to misread.

similar.title: 〜は言うに及ばず
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「及ばず」 is the classical negative of 「及ぶ」. 「言うに及ばず」 means “needless to say,” introducing an additional item (“not to mention X, even Y”). It is a coordinating usage, unlike 「に及んで」, which marks a stage in time.

formation: The particle 「に」 (marking the point reached) + the te-form 「及んで」 of the verb 「及ぶ」 (to reach, to extend). 「に」 marks the endpoint, and 「及ぶ」 means that a situation spreads step by step until it gets there, so together they mean “having spread all the way to this point.” The te-form then treats that moment as the trigger for the main clause: “and only then …” Because 「及ぶ」 itself carries a sense of gradual growth and eventual arrival, the sentence naturally feels late and critical: “it took getting this far before anything was done.” Replace the endpoint with “this last moment” (「この期」) and you get 「この期に及んで」, “at this stage of all times (and you still …).” The plain form 「に及ぶ」 and the continuative 「に及び」 keep the original meaning of “reach, extend to.”

meaning: Pairs two opposite or matching actions to show that they alternate back and forth. Mostly used in set phrases.
connection: Verb masu-stem + つ + verb masu-stem + つ

senses.label: Now … now …
senses.meaning: Two opposite actions keep alternating, as in 「行きつ戻りつ」 (pacing back and forth) and 「浮きつ沈みつ」 (bobbing up and down). It describes repetition or hesitation.
senses.connection: Opposite verbs' masu-stems + つ (行きつ戻りつ, 浮きつ沈みつ, 見えつ隠れつ)
examples: He was pacing back and forth in front of the shop.
Leaves drift down the river, bobbing up and down on the surface.

senses.label: Give and take
senses.meaning: A verb and its own passive form are paired to show both sides doing the same thing to each other, as in 「持ちつ持たれつ」 (mutual help) and 「抜きつ抜かれつ」 (neck and neck).
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + つ + same verb's passive masu-stem + つ (持ちつ持たれつ, 抜きつ抜かれつ, 追いつ追われつ)
examples: People live by helping one another.
It became a neck-and-neck race in front of the finish line.
The two talked, pouring drinks for each other.

notes: Use only the ready-made fixed pairs; do not coin your own: ✕「読みつ書きつ」「食べつ飲みつ」 → in everyday speech say 「読んだり書いたり」「食べたり飲んだり」.
Do not confuse it with 「〜つつ」: 「〜つつ」 takes a single verb and means “while …ing” or “although …”; 「〜つ〜つ」 must have two verbs in a pair and expresses alternation: ✕「行きつつ戻りつつ」 → ○「行きつ戻りつ」.
「持ちつ持たれつ」 means “mutual help, give and take” and is positive; 「抜きつ抜かれつ」 and 「追いつ追われつ」 only describe a neck-and-neck chase and carry no sense of helping each other, so they cannot be swapped.

daily.title: Between neighbors
daily.description: Said politely after neighbors help each other.
daily.example: Don't mention it. We help each other out, after all.

daily.title: Watching sports
daily.description: A commentator describes an intense match.
daily.example: The two teams put on a great neck-and-neck game.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Describing a hesitant character.
daily.example: She paced back and forth by the front door, unable to decide.

work.title: Business pleasantries
work.description: Thanking a partner and stressing mutual benefit.
work.example: We hope to maintain a mutually supportive relationship with your company.

etymology: 「つ」 is the classical auxiliary 「つ」, which marked completion. Attached to two paired verbs, it is generally thought to express two actions alternating. Modern Japanese keeps it only in set phrases.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express actions alternating or repeating. 「〜たり〜たり」 is the ordinary modern form and works with any verb (「行ったり来たりする」); 「〜つ〜つ」 is a classical remnant limited to fixed pairs, with an elegant tone mostly found in written description.

similar.title: 〜つつ
similar.explanation: Said to share an origin: 「つつ」 is thought to come from doubling the perfective 「つ」. 「〜つつ」 takes one verb and means “while …ing” or “although … (yet)” (「悪いと知りつつ」); 「〜つ〜つ」 must appear as two paired clauses and expresses two actions alternating.

formation: The stem (masu-stem) of a verb + the classical perfective auxiliary 「つ」, in two paired clauses. 「つ」 is roughly “did it for a moment”: 「行きつ」 is “went for a bit” and 「戻りつ」 is “came back for a bit.” Placing two completed mini-actions side by side creates a picture of going back and forth, “doing this, then that.” When the two verbs are opposites (「行く／戻る」, 「浮く／沈む」), the meaning is “now … now …”; when an active verb and its passive are paired (「持つ／持たれる」), it expresses reciprocity: “I do it to you, you do it to me.” Because this is a survival of classical grammar, modern Japanese keeps it only in a few fixed pairs, and you cannot coin new ones freely.

meaning: Attaches to certain nouns or adjective stems to make a verb meaning “to take on the look of …, to seem ….”
connection: Certain nouns / adjective stems + びる (大人びる, 古びる, 田舎びる, 鄙びる)

senses.label: Take on a look
senses.meaning: A person or thing naturally comes to have a certain air or condition. It isn't put on deliberately. Common as 「〜びた + noun」 or 「〜びている」.
senses.connection: 大人 / 古 / 田舎 + びる / びた / びている
examples: She seems grown-up for her age.
I stayed at a worn old inn in front of the station.
I relaxed at a rustic hot spring deep in the mountains.

senses.label: Set phrase 「悪びれる」
senses.meaning: 「悪びれる」 means “to look sheepish, to shrink back.” It is almost always negative: 「悪びれず」, 「悪びれもせず」, 「悪びれる様子もなく」, meaning “without a trace of shame.”
senses.connection: 悪びれる → 悪びれず / 悪びれもせず / 悪びれる様子もなく
examples: He showed up late without looking the least bit sorry.
The boy lied without any shame.

notes: 「〜びる」 means “naturally comes across as,” while 「〜ぶる」 means “deliberately puts on the act of”; mixing them up reverses the evaluation. 「大人びた子」 praises a child as mature and composed, whereas 「大人ぶった子」 says the child is playing grown-up, with a negative tone.

「悪びれる」 is almost only used in the negative, as 「悪びれず（に）」 or 「悪びれる様子もなく」. The latter is mostly used to criticize someone for showing no shame at all; do not mistake it for praise of someone being “composed.”

「古びた」 and 「田舎びた」 carry a negative judgment of “worn-out” or “unsophisticated,” so applying them to someone's house, clothes, or hometown is rude; 「ひなびた温泉」, on the other hand, is positive, meaning a hot spring with rustic charm.
Only a limited set of words takes 「びる」, and you cannot coin new ones: ✕「春びる」「子供びる」 → for “having a spring feel” use 「春めく」, and for “childish” use 「子供っぽい」.

daily.title: Talking about kids
daily.description: Parents chat about how their child has changed.
daily.example: Lately our daughter has suddenly started to seem grown-up.

daily.title: On a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about a hot-spring inn you stayed at.
daily.example: The inn had a rustic feel, and it was really relaxing.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Describing a character's attitude.
daily.example: The man answered “I don't know” without a hint of shame.

work.title: Real estate listing
work.description: Describing an old building.
work.example: The exterior looks old, but the interior has been fully renovated.

etymology: Generally traced to the classical suffix 「ぶ」 (as in 「大人ぶ」, 「古ぶ」), meaning “to have the look of ….” From the Edo period on it became the ichidan verb 「びる」. One theory says 「〜ぶる」 shares the same origin.

similar.title: 〜ぶる
similar.explanation: Said to share an origin, and close in form and meaning, so it is the one most easily confused. 「〜ぶる」 means deliberately putting on a certain manner and is negative (「学者ぶる」「偉ぶる」); 「〜びる」 means coming across that way naturally, with no sense of deliberateness, and is usually neutral or positive.

similar.title: 〜めく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “have the look or feel of …”. 「〜めく」 attaches to more words and often describes seasons or atmosphere (「春めく」「皮肉めいた言い方」); 「〜びる」 is limited to a few fixed words and mostly describes the appearance or air of a person or thing.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「大人っぽい」 and 「大人びた」 are often compared. 「〜っぽい」 is colloquial, widely usable, and can also express a tendency (「忘れっぽい」); 「〜びる」 is more literary and stresses maturity, age, and similar qualities that have formed naturally.

formation: A noun or the stem of an adjective + the suffix 「びる」 (from the old verb 「ぶ」). 「ぶ」 turns a noun-like quality into a verb meaning “take on the character of …”: 「大人」 becomes 「大人びる」, “take on an adult air,” and 「古（い）」 becomes 「古びる」, “take on an aged look.” Since it expresses “coming to have” rather than “deliberately putting on,” it mostly describes an appearance or air that has formed gradually, often as 「〜びた＋noun」 or 「〜びている」 for a resulting state. It is generally thought to share its origin with 「〜ぶる」 (to put on the airs of …), but 「ぶる」 added a sense of deliberate display, and the two diverged. It conjugates as an upper ichidan verb, hence 「大人びない」 and 「大人びて」.

meaning: Adds a guess to a contrast: “surely … and yet …” to show sympathy, or “if only …, it would have …” to show regret.
connection: Plain form (nouns and na-adjectives drop だ) + だろうに / でしょうに / であろうに

senses.label: Sympathy: surely … yet
senses.meaning: The speaker imagines the other person's situation (busy, tired, hard), and yet they still did something. Expresses thanks, sympathy, or concern.
senses.connection: Plain form + だろうに, 〜 (common: 「忙しいだろうに」, 「疲れているだろうに」)
examples: You must have been busy, yet you came all the way to help.
She must have been tired, but my mother welcomed me with a smile.

senses.label: Regret: if only …
senses.meaning: Used with 「〜ば」 or 「〜たら」 for a situation contrary to fact: “if …, it would have ….” It sounds regretful or reproachful. The second half is often left out, ending the sentence with 「〜だろうに」.
senses.connection: 〜ば / 〜たら + verb ta-form + だろうに (でしょうに)
examples: If we'd left a little earlier, we would have made it.
If you'd talked to me first, I could have helped.

senses.label: Sympathetic exclamation
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, it imagines someone's feelings and shows sympathy or pity. Often used with 「さぞ」.
senses.connection: さぞ + adjective / verb ta-form + だろうに
examples: After working so hard, how frustrated they must have felt.

notes: The considerate use guesses at the other person's or a third party's situation, and cannot be used for the speaker's own: ✕「私は忙しいだろうに手伝ってあげた」 → ○「私は忙しかったのに手伝ってあげた」.
「忙しいだろうに来てくれた」 is a thank-you meaning “even though you must have been busy, you made a special trip”; do not read it as “you were probably busy, so you came.” 「に」 is adversative, not causal.
The regretful use carries reproach, so saying 「相談してくだされば力になれたでしょうに」 to a superior still sounds like blaming them; to a superior say 「ご相談いただければお力になれたかと存じます」.

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: A busy friend came to see you off.
daily.example: You must be swamped with work, but thanks for coming to see me off.

daily.title: A missed bargain
daily.description: A friend missed a sale.
daily.example: If you'd come yesterday, you could have bought it cheaper.

work.title: Appreciating your team
work.description: A boss thanks a staff member who worked overtime.
work.example: You probably had plans for the weekend, so thanks for handling it. It really helped.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting that a failure could have been avoided.
work.example: Had it been inspected beforehand, the accident could have been prevented.

etymology: The conjecture auxiliary 「だろう」 + the conjunctive particle 「に」. Here 「に」 marks contrast, just like the 「に」 in 「のに」.

similar.title: 〜のに（逆接）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express contrast together with dissatisfaction or regret. 「のに」 states an accomplished fact (「雨なのに出かけた」); 「だろうに」 adds a guess to the contrast, imagining the other person's position, so it is softer and more considerate.

similar.title: 〜ば〜のに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express regret contrary to fact. 「〜ばよかったのに」 directly voices the speaker's dissatisfaction or regret; 「〜ば〜ただろうに」 focuses on guessing “what would have happened,” which is more restrained.

similar.title: 〜ものを
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “it should have been …, yet …,” with regret or reproach. 「〜ものを」 is stronger and more literary, with a heavier tone of blame (「言ってくれればいいものを」); 「だろうに」 includes a guess and is gentler.

formation: The conjectural auxiliary 「だろう」 + the adversative conjunctive particle 「に」 (the same adversative function as in 「のに」 and 「ものを」). 「だろう」 first marks the preceding clause as the speaker's guess: “(normally) it should be … right?” Then 「に」 sets that guess against the main clause, producing “it should be …, and yet in fact …”. When the guess is about the other person's situation, it becomes consideration (“you must be busy, and yet you came”); when it is about what would have resulted if things had gone differently, it becomes regret contrary to fact (“had you left earlier you would have made it, but …”). The main clause is often left out precisely because the “and yet in reality …” after 「に」 is understood by both sides, leaving a lingering sense of regret.

meaning: Says that one person or thing has two roles, qualities, or feelings at once: “both … and ….”
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + でもあり, noun / na-adjective stem + でもある (i-adjectives: 「〜くもあり〜くもある」)

senses.label: Two roles at once
senses.meaning: The same subject has two roles or qualities at the same time. The tone is objective and formal.
senses.connection: Noun + でもあり, noun + でもある
examples: He is both a doctor and a writer.
This town is both my hometown and my base for work.

senses.label: Mixed feelings
senses.meaning: Lists two different or opposite feelings to show mixed emotions. i-adjectives use 「〜くもあり〜くもある」.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + くもあり, i-adjective stem + くもある / na-adjective + でもあり〜でもある
examples: My daughter's wedding makes me both happy and a little lonely.
I'm both excited and anxious about my new life.

senses.label: であり〜でもある
senses.meaning: The first item takes 「であり」 and the second adds 「も」: “is …, and is also ….” Very common in writing.
senses.connection: Noun + であり, noun + でもある
examples: Education is a right, and also a duty.

notes: An i-adjective cannot take 「でもあり」 directly: ✕「嬉しいでもあり、寂しいでもある」 → ○「嬉しくもあり、寂しくもある」.
Both items must be two sides of the same subject. For two different people, join them with 「も」: ✕「父は医者でもあり、母は教師でもある」 → ○「父も母も教師だ」 or 「父は医者で、母は教師だ」.

It means something quite different from the similar-looking 「〜であれ〜であれ」: 「学生であれ社会人であれ参加できる」 means “whether a student or a working adult, you can join,” while 「学生でもあり社会人でもある」 means “is both a student and a working adult.”

daily.title: Graduation ceremony
daily.description: A parent talks about their child's graduation.
daily.example: Graduation is happy, but also a little sad.

daily.title: Introducing family
daily.description: Introducing your father to a friend.
daily.example: My father is both my mentor and my rival.

work.title: Introducing a speaker
work.description: Introducing a guest at an event.
work.example: Dr. Yamada is both a researcher and a business owner.

work.title: Academic writing
work.description: Discussing two sides of a concept.
work.example: Language is a tool for communication, and also culture itself.

etymology: The copula 「である」 + the particle 「も」 makes 「でもある」 (“is also”). Its continuative form 「でもあり」 links clauses, and pairing the two gives “both … and ….”

similar.title: 〜も〜ば〜も
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both say two things hold at once. 「AもBばCもD」 is mostly used to list two features of the same subject (「頭もよければ性格もいい」) and is more colloquial; 「〜でもあり〜でもある」 is used for identities, qualities, or feelings and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express “both … and …”. 「AだけでなくBも」 adds an escalation, “not only A but also B,” with the emphasis on B; 「AでもありBでもある」 treats the two items as completely equal, with no difference in weight.

similar.title: 〜であれ／〜であれ〜であれ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from the copula 「である」. 「であれ」 is the imperative form, meaning “whether it is … or …,” stressing that the condition does not affect the result; 「〜でもあり〜でもある」 affirms that both hold at the same time.

formation: Insert the particle 「も」 into the copula 「である」 to get 「でもある」 (“is also”), put the first item in the continuative 「でもあり」, and follow it with a second 「でもある」. Both items carry 「も」, meaning “is A and also B”; the two 「も」 echo each other and place A and B on an equal footing, stressing that both hold at once. With identities it means “doubles as”; with feelings, because one event triggers two emotions at the same time, it expresses a mixed “both … and …” state. I-adjectives have no 「である」, so they use the 「〜く」 form + 「も」 + 「ある」, as in 「嬉しくもあり寂しくもある」, with a fully parallel structure.

meaning: Used with a negative to mean “no matter what you try, you can't …,” with a helpless, at-a-loss tone.
connection: どうにも + negative potential / 〜ようがない; verb te-form + も + どうにもならない

senses.label: Just can't
senses.meaning: 「どうにも」 pairs with a negative potential or 「〜ようがない」: you've tried everything and still can't. More resigned than 「どうしても〜ない」.
senses.connection: どうにも + 〜できない / 〜られない / 〜ようがない
examples: I just can't stand this pain.
It's this badly broken, so there's no way to fix it.

senses.label: No use …ing
senses.meaning: 「〜てもどうにもならない」 means doing something won't change the outcome. Often used to tell someone, or yourself, to let it go.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + も + どうにもならない (今さら〜ても, 泣いても, 悩んでも)
examples: There's no point regretting it now.
Worrying about it alone won't get you anywhere.

senses.label: Just can't help feeling …
senses.meaning: With negative expressions of feeling or mood, it means “somehow I just can't …,” stressing a feeling you can't shake off.
senses.connection: どうにも + 腑に落ちない / 落ち着かない / 気が進まない, etc.
examples: His explanation just doesn't sit right with me.
I'm worried about my exam results and just can't settle down.

notes: 「どうにも」 pairs with a negative and 「どうにか」 with an affirmative, and one syllable reverses the meaning: 「どうにもならない」 is “nothing can be done,” while 「どうにかなる」 is “it will work out somehow.”
「どうにも」 must be followed by a negative or negative-sounding expression: ✕「どうにも直せる」 → ○「どうにも直せない」 / 「どうにか直せる」.
Distinguish it from 「どうしても」: 「どうしても」 can also take an affirmative to mean “by all means” (「どうしても行きたい」), but 「どうにも」 has no such use: ✕「どうにも行きたい」.
Saying 「あの人はどうにもならない」 about a person means “hopeless,” and it is very rude to say it to their face, to a superior, or to their family.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is upset about something that already happened.
daily.example: Dwelling on the past won't change anything.

daily.title: Feeling unwell
daily.description: Complaining to family about being sleepy.
daily.example: I'm so sleepy I just can't get any work done.

daily.title: Fixing something
daily.description: You find your phone is badly broken.
daily.example: The screen is cracked and I can't use it at all.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Explaining that the problem is beyond your authority.
work.example: I'm afraid this is not something I can handle with my authority.

work.title: Project meeting
work.description: Explaining that the budget can't change.
work.example: Since the budget won't increase any further, there's nothing we can do.

etymology: 「どう」 (how) + 「に」 + 「も」 (total emphasis). The original sense is “by any means at all,” which with a negative becomes “no way at all.” 「どうにもならない」 is literally “it won't turn out (well) in any way.”

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express having no way out. 「〜ようがない」 states directly that “there is no way”; 「どうにも」 is an adverb and is often combined with it for emphasis: 「どうにも直しようがない」.

similar.title: 〜てもしょうがない・〜ても仕方がない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both say doing it is pointless. 「〜ても仕方がない」 focuses on “there's no point, so better not to”; 「〜てもどうにもならない」 focuses on “it can't change the situation,” with a stronger sense of helplessness.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うにも〜ない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express being unable to do something. 「〜ようにも〜ない」 means “even wanting to, one can't,” presupposing a concrete intention; 「どうにも〜ない」 does not require a specific intention and stresses that nothing helps no matter what one tries.

formation: The interrogative adverb 「どう」 (how) + the particle 「に」 (manner) + 「も」 (universal emphasis). 「どうに」 means “in what way,” and adding 「も」 makes it “in whatever way,” so with a negative it gives “whatever I do, I can't …”. In 「〜てもどうにもならない」, 「なる」 means “to turn out (some way),” so the whole phrase reads “even if you do it, it turns out no way at all,” i.e., it is no use. When it modifies a negative of feeling (「落ち着かない」「腑に落ちない」), “no means can remove it” turns into emphasis: “really …, just can't …”.

meaning: Because of something, you end up in an unwanted, unpleasant situation: “end up having to ….”
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + 羽目になる (羽目に陥る)

senses.label: End up having to
senses.meaning: For some reason (often your own mistake or bad luck), you end up having to do something you didn't want to. Usually past tense: 「〜羽目になった」. It sounds self-mocking or regretful.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + 羽目になる / 羽目になった
examples: I lost my wallet and ended up walking home from the station.
Agreeing to it was fine, but in the end I had to do it all myself.
Because I neglected to prepare, I ended up pulling an all-nighter.

senses.label: Fall into a bad situation
senses.meaning: 「〜羽目に陥る」 is heavier and more formal, meaning someone fell into a serious predicament.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 羽目に陥る
examples: They were forced to give up their house to pay off their debts.

notes: Use it only for unwelcome bad outcomes, never good ones: ✕「宝くじに当たって、海外旅行に行く羽目になった」 → ○「…海外旅行に行くことになった」.
「羽目を外す」 means “to get carried away, let loose” and is a separate idiom unrelated to this pattern; do not mix them up just because both contain 「羽目」.
Saying 「〜羽目になりましたね」 about someone else sounds gloating or scolding; for a superior's or client's misfortune say 「〜ことになって大変でしたね」.
It attaches to a verb, not directly to a noun: ✕「残業の羽目になった」 → ○「残業する羽目になった」.

daily.title: Venting to a friend
daily.description: Telling a story about your bad luck.
daily.example: I missed the last train and ended up taking a taxi home.

daily.title: Dividing chores
daily.description: Complaining that all the chores fell to you.
daily.example: I lost at rock-paper-scissors and ended up cleaning all by myself.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Talking about overtime caused by someone else's mistake.
work.example: Because of a client's mistake, I ended up having to work on my day off.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting a company's failure.
work.example: Its reckless expansion backfired, and the company was forced to pull out.

etymology: 「羽目」 originally meant a wall made of wooden boards (羽目板). It is generally thought to have shifted to mean “situation,” especially a tight spot one is forced into; accounts of exactly how differ.

similar.title: 〜始末だ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express ending up with a bad result. 「〜始末だ」 narrates a chain of bad events and “finally even ended up …,” mostly with criticism of others; 「〜羽目になる」 mostly describes a predicament one fell into against one's will, with self-mockery.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express an outcome or arrangement. 「〜ことになる」 is neutral and works for good or bad things; 「〜羽目になる」 is only for unwelcome bad outcomes.

similar.title: 〜を余儀なくされる／〜を余儀なくさせる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express being forced into a situation. 「〜を余儀なくされる」 is literary, an objective report of being “forced to …,” and follows a noun (「中止を余儀なくされる」); 「〜羽目になる」 is more colloquial, follows a verb, and carries personal chagrin.

formation: The noun 「羽目」 (a predicament, a fix) + the case particle 「に」 (the resulting state) + 「なる」 (to become). 「〜する羽目」 uses a verb to modify 「羽目」 and spells out the predicament: “a situation where one has to do …”; 「に」 + 「なる」 expresses a result that came about naturally, stressing “I didn't choose this; events pushed me here.” That is why it is usually in the past tense, looking back on one's own bad luck with self-mockery or regret. Replace 「なる」 with 「陥る」 (to fall into) and you stress being stuck with no way out, which is heavier and more literary.

meaning: Says something isn't serious enough to call for a certain action: “not worth …, no need to ….”
connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + ほどのことではない (ほどのことでもない)

senses.label: Not worth …
senses.meaning: The matter is minor, so there's no need for a certain action. Often used to tell people not to worry or make a fuss. 「でもない」 sounds lighter.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ほどのことではない / ほどのことでもない (心配する, 騒ぐ, 怒る)
examples: It's just a little cold, so it's nothing to worry about.
It's hardly worth making such a fuss over, is it?
It's not worth going out of your way to tell people.

senses.label: Modest reply
senses.meaning: When thanked or praised, it says what you did was trivial, like “it was nothing.”
senses.connection: お礼を言われる / 褒められる + ほどのことではありません
examples: It's nothing that deserves thanks.
I haven't done anything worth praising.

notes: Saying 「騒ぐほどのことではありません」 to someone who is worried or complaining can seem to dismiss their feelings, which is especially rude toward clients or superiors; when reassuring, empathize first, then say 「大事には至らないと思います」.
The modest use applies only to what you yourself did: 「お礼を言われるほどのことではありません」. Using it to judge the other person's help amounts to saying their help was trivial: ✕「手伝ってもらったが、お礼を言うほどのことではない」.
It attaches to the dictionary form of a verb, not the nai-form: ✕「心配しないほどのことではない」 → ○「心配するほどのことではない」.

daily.title: Reassuring family
daily.description: A family member is upset over a small slip.
daily.example: It's just a broken glass. Nothing to worry about.

daily.title: Replying to thanks
daily.description: A neighbor thanks you for a small favor.
daily.example: Oh, no, it was nothing worth thanking me for.

work.title: Deciding whether to escalate
work.description: A coworker isn't sure whether to report a minor issue.
work.example: I don't think it's worth reporting to the department manager.

work.title: Handling a client
work.description: Explaining that a minor issue is no cause for concern.
work.example: It's just a slight display misalignment, so there's no need for concern.

etymology: 「ほど」 (degree) + 「の」 + the formal noun 「こと」 + the negative 「ではない」. Literally, “it isn't a matter of that degree.”

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “there's no need to …”. 「〜までもない」 gives the reason that it is obvious or simple (「言うまでもない」); 「〜ほどのことではない」 gives the reason that the matter is minor, not serious.

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can tell someone they need not do something. 「心配することはない」 speaks directly to the person, “you need not worry”; 「心配するほどのことではない」 speaks about the matter itself, “it's not that serious,” which is more objective.

similar.title: 〜には当たらない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “not so much as to …, no need to …”. 「〜には当たらない」 is more literary and mostly judges that something is “not worth being surprised at, praised, or criticized” (「驚くには当たらない」); 「〜ほどのことではない」 is common in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “no need to …”. 「〜には及ばない」 is mostly used to politely decline the other person's kindness (「ご心配には及びません」); 「〜ほどのことではない」 stresses that the matter itself is minor.

formation: 「ほど」 (degree) + 「の」 + the formal noun 「こと」 + the negative 「ではない」. 「Vするほどのこと」 means “a matter serious enough to warrant V-ing”: the verb sets a threshold of degree, and 「ではない」 says the matter does not reach it. Since what is denied is the seriousness of the matter, not the other person's action directly, the tone is an objective “it's not that serious,” leading to “there's no need to V.” Used about one's own deeds (「お礼を言われるほどのこと」), it becomes modesty: “nothing worth thanking me for.” With 「でもない」 the extra 「も」 softens it further: “hardly something worth …”.

meaning: Neither option is good, but one is a bit less bad: “would rather …, might as well ….”
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form, noun + の + ほうがましだ; often with 「〜くらいなら」 or 「〜より」

senses.label: Would rather …
senses.meaning: Rather than do something you really hate, you'd choose another option that's also bad. Often 「〜くらいなら〜ほうがましだ」. Strong tone of dislike.
senses.connection: 〜くらいなら + verb dictionary form / ta-form + ほうがましだ
examples: I'd rather die than bow my head to someone like that.
Rather than ride a packed train every day, I'd rather get up early and walk.

senses.label: Better than …
senses.meaning: 「〜よりは（も）ましだ」 means it's not good, but it's a bit better than the alternative. A negative tone.
senses.connection: Noun / verb + より（は）ましだ
examples: The room is small, but it's better than nothing.
Getting even a little sleep is better than none at all.

notes: 「まし」 does not mean “good”; it is only the lesser of two evils. Saying 「こっちのほうがましだ」 about someone's work or gift amounts to “both are bad, but this one will do,” which is very rude.
When giving advice use 「〜たほうがいい」; 「〜たほうがましだ」 sounds like “(it's bad too, but) better than …,” with distaste: ✕「早く寝たほうがましですよ」 → ○「早く寝たほうがいいですよ」.
「〜くらいなら死んだほうがましだ」 is an exaggerated, extreme expression and sounds excessive and hurtful in the workplace or when applied to someone else's choice.

daily.title: Complaining about a restaurant
daily.description: A friend is unhappy with bad food.
daily.example: If I'm paying for food like this, I'd be better off cooking myself.

daily.title: Choosing how to get there
daily.description: Discussing travel on a rainy day.
daily.example: Rather than wait in the rain, we're better off taking a taxi.

work.title: Discussing options
work.description: Comparing two less-than-ideal plans in a meeting.
work.example: Releasing at least part of it would be better than postponing everything.

etymology: 「まし」 is generally thought to come from 「増し」, the masu-stem of the verb 「増す」 (to increase), originally meaning “more, superior.” In modern Japanese it usually means “(not good, but) relatively better.”

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: Same origin: both compare two options with 「ほうが」, so they are often contrasted. 「〜ほうがいい」 is a positive piece of advice or judgment; 「〜ほうがましだ」 is the lesser of two evils, with dissatisfaction or distaste.

similar.title: 〜だけましだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「まし」. 「〜だけましだ」 picks out one thing to be thankful for within a bad situation (“at least …”); 「〜ほうがましだ」 compares and chooses between two options.

similar.title: 〜くらいなら
similar.explanation: Related in meaning, and often paired as 「〜くらいなら〜ほうがましだ」. 「〜くらいなら」 raises the option the speaker is extremely unwilling to take, and 「〜ほうがましだ」 gives the side they would rather choose.

formation: 「ほう」 (one of two sides) + 「が」 + the na-adjective 「まし」 (somewhat better) + 「だ」. In a comparison, 「ほう」 first splits the choices into two and points to “this side”; 「まし」 originally meant “to increase, to surpass,” but in modern Japanese it means “(among bad things) the lesser evil.” Together they mean “this side is the lesser evil,” which presupposes that neither option is good, so the phrase naturally carries resignation and distaste. With 「〜くらいなら」, the speaker puts the option they least want first and then uses 「ほうがましだ」 for “I'd rather choose this one.”

meaning: Doing something without limits, as much as you like, or leaving a situation to get worse without control.
connection: Verb masu-stem / verb tai-form + 放題; noun / na-adjective + 放題 (好き放題)

senses.label: All you can …
senses.meaning: For a set price, you can do something without limit. Mostly for food, drinks, and services. Neutral or even positive.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 放題 (食べ放題, 飲み放題, 使い放題, 見放題)
examples: This restaurant is all-you-can-eat for 2,000 yen.
With this plan, you get unlimited data.

senses.label: Do as one pleases
senses.meaning: Doing whatever you want with no restraint. Usually critical. Common: 「言いたい放題」, 「やりたい放題」, 「好き放題」.
senses.connection: Verb tai-form + 放題 / 好き放題, 勝手放題
examples: He said whatever he wanted at the meeting and then left.
When their parents are away, the kids do whatever they like.

senses.label: Left to run wild
senses.meaning: Something is left unattended, and a (bad) state keeps getting worse, like “gone to ruin” or “grown out of control.”
senses.connection: Intransitive verb masu-stem + 放題 (荒れ放題, 伸び放題, 散らかり放題)
examples: The garden of the empty house has gone completely wild.
I've been so busy that my hair has grown out of control.

notes: Apart from service terms such as 「食べ放題」 and 「飲み放題」, forms like 「言いたい放題」, 「やりたい放題」, and 「好き放題」 are all criticisms; saying 「言いたい放題だ」 about a superior or client is rude.
To mean “as much as one wants to do,” use the tai-form: ✕「言う放題」 → ○「言いたい放題」; for services use the masu-stem: 「食べ放題」.
Distinguish it from 「〜っぱなし」: forgetting to turn off a light is 「電気をつけっぱなし」 (left as is, the state continuing), and ✕「電気をつけ放題」.
In Japan, 「食べ放題」 is mostly time-limited, and many restaurants charge extra for too much leftover food; 「放題」 does not mean you may waste freely.

daily.title: Inviting a friend to eat
daily.description: Suggesting an all-you-can-eat place.
daily.example: Want to go to an all-you-can-eat yakiniku place this weekend?

daily.title: A parent complaining
daily.description: A child's room is a mess.
daily.example: My son's room is such a mess there's nowhere to step.

daily.title: Reading comments online
daily.description: Commenting on what a celebrity said.
daily.example: People online are saying whatever they like about him.

work.title: Planning a work party
work.description: Confirming the course for a group dinner.
work.example: I booked a course with two hours of all-you-can-drink.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Criticizing poor management.
work.example: Oversight was lax, and some employees did whatever they wanted.

etymology: 「放」 means letting go, leaving unrestrained. 「放題」 originally described doing as one pleases without restraint. Later, businesses used it for unlimited services, and words like 「食べ放題」 became widespread.

similar.title: 〜っぱなし
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both carry the sense of “leaving as is,” and both 「放題」 and 「放し（っぱなし）」 contain 「放」. 「〜っぱなし」 means something that should have been finished was not and the state continues (「開けっぱなし」); 「〜放題」 means no restraint or leaving things to get worse.

similar.title: 〜三昧
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean doing something to one's heart's content. 「〜三昧」 means being absorbed in and enjoying something (「読書三昧」「贅沢三昧」), mostly neutral or self-deprecating; 「〜放題」 stresses having no limits and doing as one pleases, mostly with criticism.

similar.title: 〜まくる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean doing something without restraint. 「〜まくる」 is slangy and stresses vigorous, frequent action (「食べまくる」); 「〜放題」 stresses the state of “no limit, free to do as one likes.”

formation: 「放題」 is made of 「放」 (to let go, to leave unrestrained) and 「題」, and as one noun means “a state of being left alone, doing as one pleases.” After the masu-stem of a verb, it means “let the action run free,” i.e., as much as you like; shops borrowed this to produce the neutral sense of “unlimited” (「食べ放題」). After the tai-form (「言いたい放題」), it stresses “giving free rein to one's own desires,” i.e., with no restraint, usually critically. After a non-volitional verb (「荒れ放題」「伸び放題」), it means “letting the change go on unchecked,” i.e., going to ruin or growing wild. All three meanings come from the same core of “leaving things unrestrained.”

title: 〜こそ〜が (concession)
meaning: First admits one fact, then turns to stress another: “… may be …, but ….”
connection: Noun + こそ + predicate + が / けれど; verb masu-stem + こそ + する / しない + が

senses.label: Noun + こそ〜が
senses.meaning: Admits the first point (often a flaw or surface impression), then gives a contrasting, more important judgment. The focus is on the second half.
senses.connection: Noun + こそ + adjective / verb + が (けれど), 〜
examples: He may have a sharp tongue, but he's kind at heart.
This place is pricey, but the food is reliably good.
He may be small, but he's second to none in strength.

senses.label: Verb + こそ + する
senses.meaning: Put a verb's masu-stem before 「こそ」 and follow with 「する / しない」: “didn't exactly …, but ….”
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + こそ + する / しない / した / しなかった + が
examples: We didn't win the game, but we played well.
He doesn't say it out loud, but inside he's happy.

notes: The first clause is the conceded part and the second is the real assessment; reversing them reverses the meaning: 「値段こそ高いが、味は確かだ」 is praise, while 「味こそ確かだが、値段が高すぎる」 is criticism.
Without 「が／けれど」, 「こそ」 is mere emphasis meaning “precisely …”: 「彼こそ優しい」 (he is the one who is truly kind) means something completely different from 「彼は口こそ悪いが、優しい」.
A verb must take the masu-stem + 「こそ」 + 「する／しない」: ✕「勝ったこそしなかったが」「勝つこそしなかったが」 → ○「勝ちこそしなかったが」.

daily.title: Introducing a friend
daily.description: Introducing a blunt friend to someone.
daily.example: He may talk tough, but he really looks out for people.

daily.title: Rating a restaurant
daily.description: Recommending a small place to a friend.
daily.example: The place may be tiny, but the food is the real deal.

work.title: Evaluating a new hire
work.description: A manager comments on a new employee to a colleague.
work.example: She may be short on experience, but she picks things up fast.

work.title: Explaining a product
work.description: Describing a product's features to a client.
work.example: The price may be on the high side, but its durability is outstanding.

etymology: 「こそ」 is an emphatic particle. In classical Japanese, 「こそ」 required the sentence to end in the realis form (kakari-musubi), and when 「こそ + realis form」 appeared mid-sentence it often expressed a concession. Modern Japanese keeps that concessive use as 「こそ〜が」.

similar.title: 〜こそ〜が（although … but）
similar.explanation: Another entry with the same structure and essentially the same meaning, so compare the two. Both stress that the first clause is only a concession and the point lies in the second.

similar.title: 〜こそ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use the focus particle 「こそ」. 「こそ」 alone only expresses emphasis, “precisely …, it is … that …” (「今年こそ合格したい」); in this pattern 「こそ」 pairs with 「が」 to express a concession.

similar.title: 〜こそすれ／〜こそあれ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「こそ」. 「〜こそすれ〜ない」 means “will do …, but never …,” denying the second clause (「感謝こそすれ、恨むことはない」); 「〜こそ〜が」 concedes the first clause and then turns, so both clauses hold.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express concession and contrast. 「〜ものの」 concedes the whole preceding clause (「買ったものの、使っていない」); 「こそ〜が」 uses 「こそ」 to concede only one aspect, so the focus is clearer.

formation: The focus particle 「こそ」 + a predicate + the adversative 「が／けれど」. The basic job of 「こそ」 is to single out one element; here it picks out one aspect of the first clause (the mouth, the price) to say “as far as this point goes, it is indeed …”. The 「が」 that follows turns the sentence: “but the other (more important) aspects are …”. In other words, 「こそ」 draws the boundary of the concession, and the second clause gives the real assessment outside it. A verb cannot take 「こそ」 directly, so it becomes the masu-stem and is picked up by 「する／しない」, forming 「勝ちこそしなかったが」. This use is generally thought to descend from the classical 「こそ＋已然形」 kakari-musubi, which expressed contrast within a sentence.

meaning: Gives one of the reasons for a result and hints that there are others: “partly because ….”
connection: Plain form (noun / na-adjective + という / な) + こともあって (こともあり)

senses.label: One reason among others
senses.meaning: Gives one reason while hinting “there are others too.” Softer than 「〜ので」. The second half is an objective result, not a command or intention.
senses.connection: Plain form + こともあって; noun + ということもあって
examples: Partly because it was the weekend, the shop was extremely crowded.
Partly because it was raining, there were fewer customers than usual.

senses.label: Written 「こともあり」
senses.meaning: In writing and news, the continuative form 「こともあり」 is common, with the same meaning.
senses.connection: Plain form + こともあり, 〜
examples: Partly because it was my first business trip abroad, I was quite nervous.
Partly due to the weak yen, the number of foreign tourists is rising.

notes: The main clause can only be an event that has happened or an objective result, not a request, command, or volition: ✕「雨ということもあって、早く帰ってください」 → ○「雨なので、早く帰ってください」.
Nouns and na-adjectives need 「という」 or 「な」: ✕「週末こともあって」 → ○「週末ということもあって」.
Distinguish it from 「〜こともある」 (sometimes …): 「遅れることもある」 is “sometimes I am late,” while 「遅れたこともあって」 is “partly because I was late.”
When apologizing to a client, listing reasons first with 「〜こともあって」 can sound like making excuses; apologize first, then explain.

daily.title: Talking about a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about your travels.
daily.example: Partly because it was a long weekend, everywhere was packed.

daily.title: Explaining how you feel
daily.description: Explaining why you're so tired today.
daily.example: Partly because I didn't sleep much last night, I'm sleepy today.

work.title: Sales report
work.description: Analyzing why sales went up.
work.example: Thanks to the new products and partly to the hot weather, sales grew.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting on traffic.
work.example: Partly because it coincided with the holiday rush, the expressway was badly jammed.

etymology: The formal noun 「こと」 + 「も」 (also) + the te-form of 「ある」. 「も」 hints “not just this reason,” which gives the sense of “one of the reasons.”

similar.title: 〜ことだし
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both hint at “there are other reasons too.” 「〜ことだし」 is mostly followed by the speaker's decision or suggestion (「雨も降っていることだし、帰ろう」); 「〜こともあって」 is followed by an objective result and cannot take volition.

similar.title: 〜とあって／〜とあっては
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both give a reason. 「〜とあって」 stresses the natural result of a special circumstance (「連休とあって、どこも混んでいる」); 「〜こともあって」 only names one of the reasons and does not stress anything special.

similar.title: 〜せいか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both give a reason gently. 「〜せいか」 carries uncertainty (“perhaps because …”) and is mostly for bad results; 「〜こともあって」 gives one definite reason, and the result can be good or bad.

formation: The formal noun 「こと」 + the particle 「も」 + the te-form 「あって」 of the verb 「ある」. 「こと」 turns the whole preceding clause into “this fact,” 「ある」 says “this fact exists,” and the te-form introduces it as the reason for the main clause: “because there is this fact.” The key is 「も」: “there is also this fact,” which hints that this is not the only reason, so the tone is gentler and more objective than 「ので」 or 「から」 and suits narrating an established result. In writing, 「あって」 is replaced by the continuative 「あり」 with the same structure.

meaning: Expresses acting to keep something bad from happening: “so as not to …, to avoid ….” Formal in tone.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ことのないように (ことのないよう, ことがないように)

senses.label: So as not to …
senses.meaning: Taking action to prevent a bad outcome. More formal than 「〜ないように」. Often used in apologies and resolutions.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことのないよう（に）+ 努める / 注意する / 〜する
examples: We will work to prevent this from happening again so that the same mistake is never repeated.
I explained carefully so as not to cause any misunderstanding.

senses.label: Reminders and requests
senses.meaning: Used in notices and announcements to ask people to be careful about something. Followed by 「お願いします」, 「ご注意ください」, etc.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことのないよう + お願いいたします / ご注意ください
examples: Please make sure not to miss the deadline.
Please be careful not to leave your valuables behind.

notes: Attach it to the affirmative dictionary form of a verb, since 「ない」 already carries the negation; adding another negation makes a double negative and reverses the meaning: ✕「遅れないことのないように」 → ○「遅れることのないように」.
Even though it is formal, 「〜ことのないようにしてください」 is still a command; to a superior or client say 「〜ことのないよう、お願いいたします」 or 「ご注意いただけますと幸いです」.
In everyday speech 「〜ないように」 is enough; saying 「忘れることのないように」 to a friend sounds stiff, like a public notice.

daily.title: Reading a notice
daily.description: Seeing an apartment reminder about garbage sorting.
daily.example: Please be careful not to get the collection day wrong.

daily.title: A note to yourself
daily.description: Writing a resolution in your diary.
daily.example: I'll leave a note so I don't make the same mistake again.

work.title: Letter of apology
work.description: A company apologizes to customers and promises improvement.
work.example: We will thoroughly train our staff so that this never happens again.

work.title: Meeting notice
work.description: Reminding attendees of rules.
work.example: Please be sure not to be late on the day.

etymology: The formal noun 「こと」 + the subject particle 「の」 (= が) + 「ない」 + 「ように」 for purpose. Literally, “so that the thing … does not happen.”

similar.title: 〜ように（目的）
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use the purpose 「ように」. 「〜ないように」 is the ordinary form, fine in speech and writing; 「〜ことのないように」 adds the formal noun 「こと」 and is more formal and literary.

similar.title: 〜ことなく
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are made of 「こと」 + 「ない」. 「〜ことなく」 describes what actually happens, “without …ing, (and instead) …” (「休むことなく働いた」); 「〜ことのないように」 expresses the purpose of preventing something from happening.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express purpose. 「〜ために」 mostly means actively doing something to achieve a goal (「合格するために」); 「〜ことのないように」 is specifically for preventing something bad from happening.

formation: The formal noun 「こと」 + the subject marker 「の」 (= 「が」) + 「ない」 + the purpose 「ように」. 「〜ことがない」 means “it doesn't happen that …”; when modifying a following word, 「が」 changes to 「の」, giving 「〜ことのない」. Adding 「ように」, which marks a goal state, gives “so that the state of ‘… not happening’ is achieved.” Compared with 「〜ないように」, the extra 「こと」 abstracts a concrete action into a “state of affairs,” which sounds more objective and formal, and is why it suits notices, regulations, and promises of non-recurrence in apologies.

meaning: Says only one person or thing fits the description: “only … would …, … is about all.”
connection: Noun + くらい (ぐらい) のものだ

senses.label: Only … would
senses.meaning: Limits it to a person: only this person does something (special or unusual). Often 「〜のは〜くらいのものだ」, implying “nobody else would.”
senses.connection: 〜のは + noun (person) + くらいのものだ
examples: Only he would take on such an unreasonable order.
The only one who gets up at five every morning to run is my father.

senses.label: … is about all
senses.meaning: Limits a thing or amount: count as you may, that's all there is, implying “it's not much to speak of.”
senses.connection: Noun + くらいのものだ (often with 「〜といえば」 or 「〜のは」)
examples: On my days off, about all I do is take walks.
Curry is about the only dish I can make.

notes: Distinguish it from the 「くらい」 meaning “about”: 「千円くらいのもの」 is “something costing about a thousand yen,” whereas this pattern limits to “only …”: 「そんなことをするのは彼くらいのものだ」.

When limiting persons it often carries the nuance “only he would do such a (strange) thing,” which can be praise or criticism; saying 「〜するのは部長くらいのものです」 to a superior may be heard as sarcasm, so mind the tone.
About oneself it is modest (「趣味は散歩くらいのものです」), but used to judge the other person's things or abilities it is belittling: ✕「あなたが作れるのはカレーくらいのものだ」.

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Saying only one person at home likes something.
daily.example: The only one at home who eats natto is my mom.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: A friend asks what your hobbies are.
daily.example: Hobbies? Watching a movie now and then is about it.

work.title: Praising a coworker
work.description: Praising someone's exceptional ability.
work.example: Only Sato-san could pull off such a tough negotiation.

etymology: 「くらい」 comes from the noun 「位（くらい）」, meaning rank or degree. Combined with 「のものだ」, it means “something only of this degree (range),” which gives the limiting sense.

similar.title: 〜をおいて
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both limit to “only …”. 「〜をおいて〜ない」 is literary and formal, mostly high praise (「彼をおいて適任者はいない」); 「〜くらいのものだ」 is more colloquial, can be praise or criticism, and can also mean “just this much, that's all.”

similar.title: 〜しか〜ない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express limitation. 「〜しか〜ない」 limits objectively with a negative sentence; 「〜くらいのものだ」 uses an affirmative sentence with a subjective evaluation of “rare” or “not worth mentioning.”

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい（belittling / minimum）
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use the belittling nuance of 「くらい」. 「〜くらい」 alone means “a mere …, at least this little thing” (「挨拶くらいしなさい」); 「〜くらいのものだ」 comes at the end of the sentence and limits to “only this, just this much.”

formation: 「くらい」 (degree, extent) + 「の」 + the formal noun 「もの」 + 「だ」. 「Nくらいのもの」 is “something at the level of N,” where 「くらい」 draws a very narrow range; 「ものだ」 then asserts about it: “what fits the condition is just this.” The sentence thus becomes “count them up, and it's only N / only this.” When limiting people, it implies that no one else can, giving the assessment “only he can”; when limiting things, the belittling sense of 「くらい」 (“nothing much”) comes to the surface and it becomes “just …, that's all.”

meaning: After a verb's masu-stem, it means doing something over and over without restraint. Very casual.

senses.label: Go all out
senses.meaning: Actively doing something a lot, again and again, like “like crazy” or “nonstop.” Casual slang.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + まくる (食べまくる, 遊びまくる, しゃべりまくる, 買いまくる)
examples: I played nonstop every day during summer vacation.
I ate tons of delicious food on my trip.
She talked nonstop for a whole hour.

senses.label: One after another
senses.meaning: With non-volitional or passive verbs, something keeps happening to an extreme degree, like 「売れまくる」 or 「怒られまくる」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem (incl. passive) + まくる (売れまくる, 勝ちまくる, 怒られまくる)
examples: The new product is selling like crazy.
I've been getting chewed out by my boss all day since this morning.

notes: It is very casual slang, and using it with superiors, clients, or in formal writing sounds childish and inappropriate: ✕「資料を読みまくりました」 → ○「資料を何度も読み込みました」.
The 「まくる」 in 「腕をまくる」 and 「袖をまくる」 is the main verb “to roll up,” not this pattern.
It generally does not attach to stative or potential verbs: ✕「いまくる」「わかりまくる」; the passive (「怒られまくる」) is fine.

daily.title: Talking about vacation
daily.description: Telling a friend about a trip.
daily.example: I swam like crazy in Okinawa and got totally tanned.

daily.title: After shopping
daily.description: Regretting spending too much.
daily.example: I went on a clothes-buying spree at the sale, and now I'm broke.

daily.title: Before an exam
daily.description: Describing how you're studying.
daily.example: Exams are coming, so I'm working through past papers nonstop.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Talking about the previous day's client dinner.
work.example: At yesterday's client dinner, all I did was bow and bow and bow.

etymology: From the verb 「捲る（まくる）」, originally “to roll up, to lift,” which extended to “to push forward fiercely” (as in 「追いまくる」). As an auxiliary verb, it shows intense, repeated action.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express doing the same thing repeatedly. 「〜てばかりいる」 means “doing nothing but …” and itself carries dissatisfaction or criticism; 「〜まくる」 stresses a large amount and strong momentum, and can even carry pride when about oneself (「勉強しまくった」).

similar.title: 〜放題
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express a lack of restraint. 「〜放題」 stresses the state of “no limit, free to do as one likes” (「食べ放題」); 「〜まくる」 stresses the action actually done being vigorous and frequent.

similar.title: 〜尽くす
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean doing an action to the extreme. 「〜尽くす」 means “… all up, … completely,” stressing exhausting it with nothing left (「食べ尽くす」); 「〜まくる」 stresses force and number of repetitions, and is slang.

formation: The masu-stem of a verb + the auxiliary 「まくる」 (捲る: to roll up, also to push relentlessly forward). The main verb 「まくる」 is like rolling cloth up layer by layer, with a dynamic sense of continuity, force, and not stopping; as an auxiliary after another verb it adds that momentum to the action: 「食べまくる」 is “eat one thing after another, ravenously.” After non-volitional verbs or passives, where the subject has no control, it becomes “over and over without end, again and again” (「売れまくる」「怒られまくる」). Because the nuance is exaggerated and energetic, it is slang.
